text: Lesson 6 named H_C and H_B without defining them precisely. Here you'll write both out explicitly as sums of Pauli operators, see exactly why the mixer is almost always built from Pauli-X, and confirm why the two unitaries can't simply be merged into one.

On a quantum computer, the Pauli-Z operator on qubit i has eigenvalues plus 1 and minus 1, exactly matching an Ising spin. So the Max-Cut cost Hamiltonian becomes H_C equals the sum over edges of one-half times the identity minus Z_i Z_j. Z_0 Z_1 has eigenvalue plus 1 on states 00 and 11, same spin direction, and minus 1 on 01 and 10, opposite directions -- giving cost 0 and cost 1 respectively, exactly matching Lesson 6's simulation. Every Z_i Z_j term commutes with every other, so the cost unitary is a simple product of per-edge phase gates, no approximation needed.

The standard mixer Hamiltonian is H_B equals the sum of single-qubit Pauli-X operators. Why X specifically? Because X flips a qubit's state between 0 and 1 -- exactly the move needed to move probability amplitude between candidate bitstrings. Z-based phases alone can never change measurement probabilities on their own; only an operator that rotates between 0 and 1 can actually redistribute where the probability mass sits. And because H_B has no cross-qubit terms, its unitary factors cleanly into one independent rotation per qubit -- cheap to implement at any qubit count.

H_C and H_B must not commute, and the reason traces straight to a single-qubit fact: the commutator of Z and X equals 2i times Y, which is not zero. If they did commute, applying them in either order would produce the identical operator, and alternating them would be pointless. This non-commutation is what makes the alternating structure meaningful: each cost layer imprints problem-specific phase information, and each mixer layer converts some of that phase into redistributed probability.

Next lesson turns to the classical algorithm sitting outside the quantum computer whose entire job is finding good values of gamma and beta -- and to being honest that this subproblem is harder than it first looks.
